claim: rpg-1 is an EMS-induced mutant of M. truncatula accession A17 that was previously reported to develop enlarged ITs and poorly colonized nodules.
source: An ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-induced mutant of M. truncatula accession A17 (hereafter named rpg-1, Figure 1A) was previously reported to develop enlarged ITs and poorly colonized nodules (Arrighi et al., 2008), indicating that RPG is required for rhizobial infection.
evidence: The claim cites Arrighi et al., 2008 as the source of the previous report.

claim: RPG is required for rhizobial infection.
source: An ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-induced mutant of M. truncatula accession A17 (hereafter named rpg-1, Figure 1A) was previously reported to develop enlarged ITs and poorly colonized nodules (Arrighi et al., 2008), indicating that RPG is required for rhizobial infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phenotype of the rpg-1 mutant.

claim: rpg-2 is a homozygous mutant allele isolated from the M. truncatula Tnt1 transposon insertion collection in the R108 accession carrying an insertion at 948 bp downstream of the start codon.
source: In order to genetically confirm this function, we isolated a second independent, homozygous mutant allele from the M. truncatula Tnt1 transposon insertion collection in the R108 accession carrying an insertion at 948 bp downstream of the start codon (NF11990, hereafter named rpg-2, Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the mutant isolation and Figure 1A showing the mutation position.

claim: Both rpg mutant alleles show similar alterations of IT morphology, with ITs showing a distinctive bulbous and thick appearance compared to straight and thin ITs of their corresponding wild-types.
source: Confocal imaging of infected root hairs 35 days post-inoculation (dpi) with a fluorescent GFP-tagged strain of the compatible symbiont S. meliloti (S. meliloti-GFP) revealed similar alterations of IT morphology in both rpg mutants, with ITs showing a distinctive bulbous and thick appearance compared to straight and thin ITs of their corresponding wild-types (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The diameter of ITs formed in roots of the rpg mutants was highly variable, and significantly wider at all measure points compared to wild-types.
source: While the diameter size of ITs developed by the wild-types had little variation (Figure 1D), reflecting the tight regulation exerted by the host over the development of this tubular structure, the diameter of ITs formed in roots of the rpg mutants was highly variable, and significantly wider at all measure points (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The IT phenotype in rpg mutants indicates a loss of stringent host-controlled IT maintenance.
source: This indicates a loss of stringent host-controlled IT maintenance in these mutants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the variability and increased diameter of ITs in rpg mutants.

claim: All four genotypes (rpg-1, rpg-2, and their corresponding wild-types) showed similar root hair diameters.
source: All four genotypes showed similar root hair diameters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), whose mean values and variability are in line with a previous study reporting on the diameter of mature root hairs in M. truncatula A17 WT (Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and comparison with Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: The similar root hair diameters confirm a specific role for RPG during infection, which is consistent with its previously reported expression pattern.
source: This confirms a specific role for RPG during infection, which is consistent with its previously reported expression pattern (Arrighi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the root hair diameter data and cites Arrighi et al., 2008 for the expression pattern.

claim: ITs within cortical cells appeared consistently enlarged and bulbous in roots of both rpg mutants alleles compared to their wild-type genotypes.
source: Similar to what we observed in root hairs, ITs within cortical cells appeared consistently enlarged and bulbous in roots of both rpg mutants alleles compared to their wild-type genotypes, indicating that RPG is required to control IT development in both epidermal and cortical cell layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: RPG is required to control IT development in both epidermal and cortical cell layers.
source: Similar to what we observed in root hairs, ITs within cortical cells appeared consistently enlarged and bulbous in roots of both rpg mutants alleles compared to their wild-type genotypes, indicating that RPG is required to control IT development in both epidermal and cortical cell layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the IT phenotype in both epidermal and cortical cells.

claim: The total amount of nodular structures and the number of infected nodules were significantly reduced in both rpg mutant alleles compared to their corresponding wild-types.
source: We found that nodular structures formed on roots of both rpg mutant alleles but their total amount and the number of infected nodules were significantly reduced compared to their corresponding wild-types.
evidence: The claim is supported by nodulation capacity quantification.

claim: rpg mutants failed to develop fully elongated nodules and formed mainly bumps at 21 dpi.
source: In addition, rpg mutants failed to develop fully elongated nodules and formed mainly bumps at this time point (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by nodulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: RPG is not required to initiate nodule organogenesis but is essential for efficient infection and full colonization.
source: This further supports the hypothesis that RPG is not required to initiate nodule organogenesis but is essential for efficient infection and full colonization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the nodulation phenotype of rpg mutants.

claim: Nodulation defects were more pronounced in rpg-2 than in rpg-1, which correlates with previous findings showing that a mutation within the infection-related gene LIN affects more severely nodule development when occurring in the genetic background R108 compared to A17.
source: Nodulation defects were more pronounced in rpg-2 than in rpg-1, which well correlates with previous findings showing that a mutation within the infection-related gene LIN, which is required for IT growth, affects more severely nodule development when occurring in the genetic background R108 compared to A17 (Guan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of nodulation defects and cites Guan et al., 2013.

claim: TEM micrographs of nodule-infected cells revealed larger IT structures present in nodule tissues of rpg-1 compared to WT but WT-like cell organization and symbiosome morphology.
source: TEM micrographs of nodule-infected cells revealed larger IT structures present in nodule tissues of rpg-1 compared to WT but WT-like cell organization and symbiosome morphology (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Nodular ITs formed in rpg-1 nodules were significantly wider compared to WT.
source: By measuring the diameter of nodular ITs we found that those formed in rpg-1 nodules were significantly wider compared to WT (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Normal IT development in nodules requires RPG, but bacterial release and differentiation are not directly dependent on this gene.
source: This indicates that normal IT development in nodules requires RPG, but bacterial release and differentiation are not directly dependent on this gene.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the TEM observations of nodule tissues.

claim: RPG is essential to sustain efficient bacterial infection in M. truncatula and supports a role in controlling proper assembly and progression of infection thread structures in host root tissues.
source: Altogether these data genetically confirm that RPG is essential to sustain efficient bacterial infection in M. truncatula and clearly supports a role in controlling proper assembly and progression of infection thread structures in host root tissues.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the genetic and phenotypic data presented.

claim: RPG encodes a 1255 aa long protein with an N-terminal segment containing a putative nuclear localization signal (NLS) and an N-terminal C2 domain (NT-C2) predicted to mediate membrane tethering, linked by a serine-rich intrinsically disordered region (IDR) to a long alpha-helical C-terminal extension with several predicted coiled-coil (CC) regions possibly mediating oligomerization.
source: RPG encodes a 1255 aa long protein with an N-terminal segment containing a putative nuclear localization signal (NLS) and an N-terminal C2 domain (NT-C2) predicted to mediate membrane tethering (Zhang and Aravind, 2010), linked by a serine-rich intrinsically disordered region (IDR) to a long alpha-helical C-terminal extension with several predicted coiled-coil (CC) regions possibly mediating oligomerization (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein structure analysis shown in Figure 2A and cites Zhang and Aravind, 2010 for the NT-C2 domain function.

claim: A similar structural organization and high degrees of sequence conservation of the NT-C2 domain and the N-terminal part of the coiled-coil region were found in several homologous proteins.
source: A similar structural organization and high degrees of sequence conservation of the NT-C2 domain and the N-terminal part of the coiled-coil region were found in several homologous proteins (Arrighi et al., 2008, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and cites Arrighi et al., 2008.

claim: Composite plants expressing mCherry-RPG-FL phenocopied the WT-like IT morphology, indicating that N-terminal tagging does not impair protein functionality during IT development within root hairs.
source: Composite plants expressing mCherry-RPG-FL phenocopied the WT-like IT morphology, indicating that N-terminal tagging does not impair protein functionality during IT development within root hairs (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: The sole coiled-coil region of RPG (mCherry-RPG-CC) was able to significantly restore the morphological defects of rpg-1 ITs, even though with lower efficiency when directly compared to RPG-FL.
source: Interestingly, we found that the sole coiled-coil region of RPG (mCherry-RPG-CC) was equally able to significantly restore the morphological defects of rpg-1 ITs, even though with lower efficiency when directly compared to RPG-FL (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: Expression of mCherry-RPG-tCC did not rescue the rpg-1 IT phenotype.
source: This ability was fully dependent on the N-terminal 143 aa of this region, as expression of mCherry-RPG-tCC did not rescue the rpg-1 IT phenotype (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: Major molecular determinants conferring functionality to RPG reside in its coiled-coil domain.
source: These data suggest that major molecular determinants conferring functionality to RPG reside in its coiled-coil domain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the complementation assay results.

claim: The mCherry-NT variant alone did not restore normal IT growth in the rpg-1 mutant.
source: This was further supported by the fact that the mCherry-NT variant alone did not restore normal IT growth in the rpg-1 mutant (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: The lower complementation efficacy of mCherry-RPG-CC compared to mCherry-RPG-FL indicates the relevance of the N-terminal region for full RPG functionality.
source: On the other side, the lower complementation efficacy of mCherry-RPG-CC compared to mCherry-RPG-FL (Figure 2C) clearly indicates the relevance of the N-terminal region for full RPG functionality and further suggests that the NLS, the NT-C2 domain, and the disordered region might constitute an important regulatory unit required to fine-tune the protein function or regulate its stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the complementation assay results.

claim: The NLS, the NT-C2 domain, and the disordered region might constitute an important regulatory unit required to fine-tune the protein function or regulate its stability.
source: On the other side, the lower complementation efficacy of mCherry-RPG-CC compared to mCherry-RPG-FL (Figure 2C) clearly indicates the relevance of the N-terminal region for full RPG functionality and further suggests that the NLS, the NT-C2 domain, and the disordered region might constitute an important regulatory unit required to fine-tune the protein function or regulate its stability.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the complementation assay results.

claim: Following rhizobial inoculation, the RPG protein consistently coalesced into a few discrete cytoplasmic puncta that were visible in both uninfected and infected root hairs imaged 4–7 dpi.
source: Following rhizobial inoculation, the RPG protein consistently coalesced into a few discrete cytoplasmic puncta that were visible in both uninfected and infected root hairs imaged 4–7 dpi (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In uninfected root hairs, RPG puncta were found in the vicinity of the tip.
source: In uninfected root hairs, such puncta were found in the vicinity of the tip (uRH; Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In curled root hairs at the early stage of infection, RPG puncta were located in close proximity to the IC, and adjacent to the entrapped bacteria.
source: while in curled root hairs at the early stage of infection, these puncta were located in close proximity to the IC, and adjacent to the entrapped bacteria (IC; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In root hairs harboring growing ITs, RPG-labeled puncta were systematically present in the perinuclear cytoplasm and associated with the tip of the extending IT.
source: In root hairs harboring growing ITs, RPG-labeled puncta were systematically present in the perinuclear cytoplasm and associated with the tip of the extending IT (IT; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IT tip-associated puncta formed a patch juxtaposed to the growing IT tip ahead of progressing bacteria.
source: Closer inspection showed that IT tip-associated puncta formed a patch juxtaposed to the growing IT tip ahead of progressing bacteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When ITs exhibited multiple branches, RPG-labeled puncta were associated with the tip of each branch.
source: When ITs exhibited multiple branches, RPG-labeled puncta were associated with the tip of each branch (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A diffuse RPG signal was also detectable in the nucleus and the cytoplasm of most, though not all, infected root hairs (18/28), but its intensity was orders of magnitudes weaker compared to the signal intensity detected in the puncta.
source: Alongside with such punctate patterning, a diffuse RPG signal was also detectable in the nucleus and the cytoplasm of most, though not all, infected root hairs (18/28), but its intensity was orders of magnitudes weaker compared to the signal intensity detected in the puncta (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: RPG preferentially accumulates in cytoplasmic puncta associated with infection sites during bacterial accommodation within root hairs.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that RPG preferentially accumulates in cytoplasmic puncta associated with infection sites during bacterial accommodation within root hairs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the localization data.

claim: The preferential accumulation of RPG in cytoplasmic puncta is in contrast to the exclusive nuclear localization previously reported for RPG when being ectopically expressed in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: This is in contrast to the exclusive nuclear localization previously reported for RPG when being ectopically expressed in N. benthamiana leaves (Arrighi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim compares the current findings with Arrighi et al., 2008.

claim: Upon constitutive, heterologous over-expression in N. benthamiana leaves, RPG signal was observed diffuse in the cytoplasm, accumulating in the nucleolus and in a few small cytoplasmic punctate structures associated to the perinuclear area but also found in other areas of pavement cells.
source: While we also observed nuclear accumulation of RPG upon constitutive, heterologous over-expression in N. benthamiana leaves, we additionally observed RPG signal diffuse in the cytoplasm, accumulating in the nucleolus and in a few small cytoplasmic punctate structures associated to the perinuclear area but also found in other areas of pavement cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-expression of RPG with the viral silencing suppressor p19 enhanced the accumulation of RPG in punctate structures, although it concurrently led to the formation of large accumulations of the fusion protein in the perinuclear area.
source: To facilitate the detection of these puncta, we co-expressed RPG with the viral silencing suppressor p19 (Voinnet et al., 2003), which reduces post-transcriptional gene silencing impeding gene expression during Agrobacterium-mediated gene transfer (Johansen and Carrington, 2001; Voinnet et al., 2003). This enhanced the accumulation of RPG in punctate structures, although it concurrently led to the formation of large accumulations of the fusion protein in the perinuclear area (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), most likely caused by the high level of transgene expression reached under co-infiltration conditions (Jay et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and cites Voinnet et al., 2003, Johansen and Carrington, 2001, and Jay et al., 2023.

claim: The coalescence of RPG in cytoplasmic puncta occurs also in N. benthamiana heterologous system, as similarly recently reported by a second independent study.
source: Thus, the coalescence of RPG in cytoplasmic puncta occurs also in N. benthamiana heterologous system, as similarly recently reported by a second independent study (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current data and cites Li et al., 2023.

claim: The coiled-coil domain is necessary and sufficient for RPG localization to discrete puncta.
source: We found that both mCherry-RPG-CC and mCherry-RPG-tCC accumulated to bright punctate structures as mCherry-RPG-FL, while the mCherry-RPG-NT signal remained diffuse in the cytoplasm and preferentially accumulated in the nucleus of transformed root hairs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D). These results indicate that the coiled-coil domain is necessary and sufficient for RPG localization to discrete puncta (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by localization analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D and Figure 3C.

claim: The deletion of amino acid residues 331–473, although abolishing its functionality, does not affect its localization to these foci.
source: and that the deletion of amino acid residues 331–473, although abolishing its functionality, does not affect its localization to these foci (Figure 2A–C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by localization and complementation data shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: The coiled-coil domain determines the preferential retention of the protein in cytoplasmic puncta.
source: In addition, the consistent nuclear accumulation of mCherry-RPG-NT compared to the diffuse nucleo-cytoplasmic localization weakly detectable for RPG-FL, suggests that the coiled-coil domain determines the preferential retention of the protein in cytoplasmic puncta (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–D and Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization patterns of different RPG constructs.

claim: Optimal targeting and/or accumulation of RPG to the IT tip relies on the presence of its N-terminal part.
source: It should, however, be noted that the accumulation of mCherry-RPG-CC at IT-tip associated puncta (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B - inset) occurred less frequently (7/22 root hairs harboring infection threads) compared to mCherry-RPG-FL (17/21 root hairs harboring infection threads), while both consistently labeled perinuclear or cytoplasmic puncta. This suggests that optimal targeting and/or accumulation of RPG to the IT tip relies on the presence of its N-terminal part (Figure 3C), which well correlates with the reduced capacity of RPG-CC to restore IT morphology in rpg-1 transgenic roots in comparison to RPG-FL (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization and complementation data.

claim: mCherry-RPG co-localized with VPY-GFP in punctate structures located at the tip of the IT and in the cytoplasm connecting the nucleus to the IT tip of infected root hairs.
source: We found that mCherry-RPG co-localized with VPY-GFP in punctate structures located at the tip of the IT and in the cytoplasm connecting the nucleus to the IT tip of infected root hairs (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–C.

claim: Co-expression of GFP-RPG with mCherry-LIN resulted in distinct co-localization of the two proteins in root hairs undergoing infection.
source: Co-expression of GFP-RPG with mCherry-LIN, the latter being transcriptionally driven by the constitutive Ubiquitin promoter from L. japonicus (pLjUbi), also resulted in distinct co-localization of the two proteins in root hairs undergoing infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–C.

claim: GFP-RPG and mCherry-RPG co-purified with mCherry-EXO70H4 and VPY-GFP, respectively, when using anti-RFP nanobody traps.
source: When using anti-RFP nanobody traps, GFP-RPG and mCherry-RPG co-purified with mCherry-EXO70H4 and VPY-GFP, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A.

claim: GFP-RPG consistently co-precipitated with mCherry-EXO70H4 when using anti-GFP nanobody traps.
source: To reciprocally validate these data, we performed these assays using anti-GFP nanobody traps. While GFP-RPG consistently co-precipitated with mCherry-EXO70H4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B),
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7B.

claim: Using VPY-GFP as bait resulted in co-precipitation of EXO70H4 but not of mCherry-RPG.
source: we were unable to pull sufficient amounts of VPY-GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C), suggesting that the majority of the VPY protein pool is not associated with RPG under these conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7C.

claim: The majority of the VPY protein pool is not associated with RPG under the conditions tested.
source: we were unable to pull sufficient amounts of VPY-GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C), suggesting that the majority of the VPY protein pool is not associated with RPG under these conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Co-IP results.

claim: VPY-positive puncta were systematically present in infected (18/19 in a total number of eight plants) and uninfected (6/8 in a total number of six plants) root hairs of transformed WT roots.
source: Indeed, while we systematically observed bright VPY-positive puncta in infected (18/19 in a total number of eight plants) and uninfected (6/8 in a total number of six plants) root hairs of transformed WT roots,
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data.

claim: A reliable signal of VPY punctate subcellular structures in rpg-1 transformed root hairs was neither detected in infected (19/19 events in a total number of 10 plants) nor in uninfected (8/8 events in a total number of seven plants) root hairs.
source: a reliable signal of such punctate subcellular structures in rpg-1 transformed root hairs was neither detected in infected (19/19 events in a total number of 10 plants) nor in uninfected (8/8 events in a total number of seven plants) root hairs. In all cases, VPY exhibited a diffuse cytoplasmic signal (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The symbiont-induced re-localization of VPY to the IT-tip and perinuclear-associated puncta is RPG-dependent.
source: From these data, we concluded that the symbiont-induced re-localization of VPY to the IT-tip and perinuclear-associated puncta is RPG-dependent (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the VPY localization data in WT and rpg-1.

claim: RPG alone is sufficient for the efficient recruitment of VPY to subcellular puncta in a symbiont-independent manner.
source: In contrast, constitutive co-expression with mCherry-RPG resulted in VPY coalescing into few punctate structures, mostly found at the perinuclear cytoplasm of root hairs, where it co-localized with RPG (43/52 root hairs in a total number of 18 plants, Figure 4C–E). This indicates that RPG alone is sufficient for the efficient recruitment of VPY to subcellular puncta in a symbiont-independent manner (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ectopic expression data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: RPG is an essential component of the infectosome complex.
source: Here, we demonstrate that RPG is an essential component of the infectosome complex (Liu et al., 2019b; Roy et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings and cites Liu et al., 2019b and Roy et al., 2020.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in RPG entirely blocks the recruitment of VPY to infectosome foci.
source: A loss-of-function mutation in RPG entirely blocks the recruitment of VPY to infectosome foci.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the VPY recruitment data.

claim: RPG provides specificity to a conserved cellular machinery that enables rhizobial accommodation.
source: Thus, we propose that RPG provides specificity to a conserved cellular machinery that enables rhizobial accommodation.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: In uninfected growing root hairs, PI(4,5)P2 enriched at the apical membrane domain.
source: In uninfected growing root hairs, PI(4,5)P2 enriched at the apical membrane domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 was locally and specifically enriched at the membrane surrounding invading bacteria emerging from the IC at the onset of infection.
source: while PI(4,5)P2 was locally and specifically enriched at the membrane surrounding invading bacteria emerging from the IC at the onset of infection (Figure 5A – IC and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5A – IC and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Symbiont accommodation coincides with membrane polarization at the host-microbe interface.
source: This indicates that symbiont accommodation coincides with membrane polarization at this host-microbe interface.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data.

claim: In root hairs harboring actively growing ITs, local enrichment of the phosphoinositide was consistently observed on the membrane surrounding the tip and the terminal part of the extending tube, connected to the nucleus by a dense column of cytoplasm.
source: In root hairs harboring actively growing ITs, we consistently observed local enrichment of the phosphoinositide on the membrane surrounding the tip and the terminal part of the extending tube, connected to the nucleus by a dense column of cytoplasm (Figure 5 – IT and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), confirming that bacterial progression is associated with strong polarization of the IT membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5 – IT and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Bacterial progression is associated with strong polarization of the IT membrane.
source: In root hairs harboring actively growing ITs, we consistently observed local enrichment of the phosphoinositide on the membrane surrounding the tip and the terminal part of the extending tube, connected to the nucleus by a dense column of cytoplasm (Figure 5 – IT and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), confirming that bacterial progression is associated with strong polarization of the IT membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data.

claim: Local PI(4,5)P2 enrichment occurred on the basal membrane of root hair cells hosting polarized ITs extending within a cytoplasmic column connected to the root hair cell base, and on the apical membrane of underlying cortical cells.
source: Notably, we observed that local PI(4,5)P2 enrichment also occurred on the basal membrane of root hair cells hosting polarized ITs extending within a cytoplasmic column connected to the root hair cell base, and on the apical membrane of underlying cortical cells (Figure 5A – CC, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5A – CC, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Local membrane polarization occurs on the trajectory of IT propagation and might serve to direct local changes in the cell wall and apoplastic space in preparation for the transcellular passage of the bacteria.
source: This suggests that local membrane polarization occurs on the trajectory of IT propagation and might serve to direct local changes in the cell wall and apoplastic space in preparation for the transcellular passage of the bacteria.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data.

claim: The apex of uninfected growing root hairs was labeled by the PI(4,5)P2 biosensor in rpg-1 as in the WT.
source: Here, the apex of uninfected growing root hairs was labeled by the PI(4,5)P2 biosensor as in the WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 patterning was similar to WT at the very initial stage of bacterial accommodation in rpg-1, where local enrichment occurred on the membrane surrounding the bacteria protruding from the IC.
source: PI(4,5)P2 patterning was also similar to WT at the very initial stage of bacterial accommodation, where we observed a local enrichment occurring on the membrane surrounding the bacteria protruding from the IC (Figure 5A – IC and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5A – IC and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: RPG is not required to establish membrane polarization at the initial stage of bacterial accommodation.
source: Thus, RPG is not required to establish membrane polarization at this stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data in rpg-1.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 failed to strongly enrich on the majority of membranes (21/33 ITs from 10 plants) of typically enlarged infection threads developed by the rpg-1 mutant.
source: However, PI(4,5)P2 failed to strongly enrich on the majority of membranes (21/33 ITs from 10 plants) of typically enlarged infection threads developed by the rpg-1 mutant. Here, the signal of the probe remained either low and uniformly labeling the membrane, cytoplasmic, or almost absent (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A), indicating that functional RPG is required to maintain IT-confined PI(4,5)P2 polarization during symbiont accommodation.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Functional RPG is required to maintain IT-confined PI(4,5)P2 polarization during symbiont accommodation.
source: However, PI(4,5)P2 failed to strongly enrich on the majority of membranes (21/33 ITs from 10 plants) of typically enlarged infection threads developed by the rpg-1 mutant. Here, the signal of the probe remained either low and uniformly labeling the membrane, cytoplasmic, or almost absent (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A), indicating that functional RPG is required to maintain IT-confined PI(4,5)P2 polarization during symbiont accommodation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data in rpg-1.

claim: Not the establishment but rather the maintenance and confinement of symbiont-induced polarization is RPG-dependent.
source: When present, the enrichment was often found on short membrane protrusions formed at multiple polar sites on the enlarged infection structures developed within rpg-1 root hairs, further supporting that not the establishment but rather the maintenance and confinement of symbiont-induced polarization is RPG-dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data in rpg-1.

claim: The development of polar domains at the base of infected root hair cells and on the apical membrane of underlying cortical cells occurred in rpg-1.
source: In addition, we found that the development of polar domains at the base of infected root hair cells and on the apical membrane of underlying cortical cells occurred in rpg-1 (Figure 5A – CC, Figure 5—figure supplements 3D and 5B), implying that RPG is not necessary for these pre-infection responses but exclusively for IT maintenance and progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5A – CC, Figure 5—figure supplements 3D and 5B.

claim: RPG is not necessary for pre-infection responses but exclusively for IT maintenance and progression.
source: In addition, we found that the development of polar domains at the base of infected root hair cells and on the apical membrane of underlying cortical cells occurred in rpg-1 (Figure 5A – CC, Figure 5—figure supplements 3D and 5B), implying that RPG is not necessary for these pre-infection responses but exclusively for IT maintenance and progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data in rpg-1.

claim: Functional RPG is important to maintain synchronization between cells during the infection process.
source: However, such responses were uncoupled from IT polarization and nuclear-guided progression of the tube within the root hair (Figure 5A-CC and Figure 5—figure supplement 5B), suggesting that functional RPG is important to maintain synchronization between cells during the infection process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PI(4,5)P2 enrichment data in rpg-1.

claim: There is a statistical difference in the Phasor position of fluorescence emission at the IT membrane but not at other domains between WT and rpg-1.
source: This analysis revealed a statistical difference in the Phasor position of fluorescence emission at the IT membrane but not at other domains, with the consistent shift towards the left part of the Phasor plot observed for rpg-1 ITs being indicative of a low PI(4,5)P2 membrane enrichment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Phasor analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3E.

claim: In WT infected root hairs, the tip-polarized enrichment of the PI(4,5)P2 biosensor on the IT membrane spatially coincided with low enrichment of the PI4P probe, which instead preferentially accumulated on the root hair plasma membrane.
source: In WT infected root hairs, the tip-polarized enrichment of the PI(4,5)P2 biosensor on the IT membrane spatially coincided with low enrichment of the PI4P probe, which instead preferentially accumulated on the root hair plasma membrane (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Differential membrane enrichment of the two biosensors was much reduced in most of rpg-1 infected root hairs, where PI4P was similarly enriched on the root hair plasma membrane and on the infection thread membrane, the latter being characterized by low accumulation of the PI(4,5)P2 probe.
source: Such differential membrane enrichment of the two biosensors was much reduced in most of rpg-1 infected root hairs, where PI4P was similarly enriched on the root hair plasma membrane and on the infection thread membrane, the latter being characterized by low accumulation of the PI(4,5)P2 probe (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: The IT tip versus plasma membrane fluorescence ratio of each biosensor in infected root hairs statistically validates the differential enrichment of the two phosphoinositides in the membrane surrounding the tip of WT and rpg-1 ITs.
source: We quantitatively confirmed these observations by assessing the IT tip versus plasma membrane fluorescence ratio of each biosensor in infected root hairs, statistically validating the differential enrichment of the two phosphoinositides in the membrane surrounding the tip of WT and rpg-1 ITs (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RPG has a role in sustaining localized membrane polarization at the tip of the IT.
source: These results support our previous set of data, indicating a role for RPG in sustaining localized membrane polarization at the tip of the IT (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the PI(4,5)P2 and PI4P enrichment data.

claim: In most of the WT root hairs hosting ITs imaged at 4–8 dpi with S. meliloti-mCherry (11/14 ITs from six plants), the nucleus and the IT were connected by EMTs extending from the nucleus and forming a cone-shaped array surrounding the IT tip, which was oriented towards the root hair base, following the nuclear trajectory.
source: In most of the WT root hairs hosting ITs imaged at 4–8 dpi with S. meliloti-mCherry (11/14 ITs from six plants), the nucleus and the IT were connected by EMTs extending from the nucleus and forming a cone-shaped array surrounding the IT tip, which was oriented towards the root hair base, following the nuclear trajectory (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When imaging rpg-1 infected root hairs, the connection between the nucleus and the IT tip appeared loosened or completely absent in the majority of cases (31/48 ITs from 14 plants).
source: When imaging rpg-1 infected root hairs, such connection appeared loosened or completely absent in the majority of cases (31/48 ITs from 14 plants). Here, EMTs mostly appeared dispersed or stretched, no longer bridging the tip and the nucleus (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that loss of nuclear-mediated IT guidance occurs in rpg-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of nuclear-mediated IT guidance occurs in rpg-1.
source: When imaging rpg-1 infected root hairs, such connection appeared loosened or completely absent in the majority of cases (31/48 ITs from 14 plants). Here, EMTs mostly appeared dispersed or stretched, no longer bridging the tip and the nucleus (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that loss of nuclear-mediated IT guidance occurs in rpg-1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the microtubule organization data.

claim: The tip of ITs formed within rpg-1 infected root hairs appeared frequently misoriented with respect to the direction of growth (19/48 ITs), pointing towards the root hair shank instead of following the repositioning of the nucleus down the root hair.
source: In addition, the tip of ITs formed within rpg-1 infected root hairs appeared frequently misoriented with respect to the direction of growth (19/48 ITs), pointing towards the root hair shank instead of following the repositioning of the nucleus down the root hair (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), further hinting for a defect in controlling IT directionality in this mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a defect in controlling IT directionality in rpg-1.
source: In addition, the tip of ITs formed within rpg-1 infected root hairs appeared frequently misoriented with respect to the direction of growth (19/48 ITs), pointing towards the root hair shank instead of following the repositioning of the nucleus down the root hair (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), further hinting for a defect in controlling IT directionality in this mutant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the IT tip orientation data.

claim: The tip-to-nucleus distance measured in infected root hairs of rpg-1 exhibited a higher variability compared to WT, with a major proportion of root hairs displaying a greater distance separating the nucleus from the IT tip.
source: The tip-to-nucleus distance measured in infected root hairs of rpg-1 exhibited a higher variability compared to WT, with a major proportion of root hairs displaying a greater distance separating the nucleus from the IT tip (Figure 6B, median value of 63, 68 μm), coinciding in most of the cases with the loss of a microtubule-based connection between these two domains (23/31 ITs, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The formation of a physical connection between the IT tip and the nucleus per se does not depend on RPG.
source: Though less frequently when compared to WT, we did observe EMTs linking the IT tip to the nucleus in rpg-1 infected root hairs, maintaining a tip-to-nucleus distance comparable to what was observed in WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the formation of a physical connection between these two poles per se does not depend on RPG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the microtubule organization data.

claim: The loss of RPG functionality perturbs the maintenance of the connection between the IT tip and the nucleus and of an optimal distancing between the nucleus and the extending tip during IT growth.
source: Rather, the loss of RPG functionality perturbs the maintenance of such connection and of an optimal distancing between the nucleus and the extending tip during IT growth (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the microtubule organization and tip-to-nucleus distance data.

claim: In WT root hairs harboring growing ITs, NPL consistently showed a preferential accumulation in the apoplastic space surrounding the tip when compared to the older parts of the IT.
source: In WT root hairs harboring growing ITs and in agreement with a previous report (Liu et al., 2019a), NPL consistently showed a preferential accumulation in the apoplastic space surrounding the tip when compared to the older parts of the IT (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6B–C and cites Liu et al., 2019a.

claim: NPL accumulated in the whole lumen of the enlarged ITs without any increased accumulation at a specific site in most rpg-1 root hairs.
source: By contrast, NPL accumulated in the whole lumen of the enlarged ITs without any increased accumulation at a specific site in most rpg-1 root hairs (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: RPG is required to restrict the secretion domain of NPL during infection.
source: This indicates that RPG is required to restrict the secretion domain of NPL during infection (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the NPL localization data.

claim: RPG is a crucial modulator of the infectosome machinery sustaining the polar growth of intracellular ITs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that RPG is a crucial modulator of the infectosome machinery sustaining the polar growth of intracellular ITs.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings.

claim: RPG coalesces with VPY and LIN in IT tip- and perinuclear-associated puncta (infectosome foci).
source: RPG coalesces with VPY and LIN in IT tip- and perinuclear-associated puncta (infectosome foci, Figure 3D–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3D–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–C.

claim: RPG is indispensable for VPY recruitment into infectosome foci during IT progression.
source: and is indispensable for VPY recruitment into these cytoplasmic structures during IT progression (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by VPY localization data shown in Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: A cooperative function of RPG with the infectosome complex in regulating IT polar growth is consistent with the phenotypes of rpg, vpy, and lin mutants, exhibiting strong defects in the establishment and/or the maintenance of IT progression but not being affected in nodule organogenesis.
source: A cooperative function of RPG with the infectosome complex in regulating IT polar growth is consistent with the phenotypes of rpg, vpy, and lin mutants, exhibiting strong defects in the establishment and/or the maintenance of IT progression but not being affected in nodule organogenesis (Kiss et al., 2009; Murray et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2019b; Li et al., 2023, Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of mutant phenotypes and cites Kiss et al., 2009, Murray et al., 2011, Liu et al., 2019b, and Li et al., 2023.

claim: The peculiar enlargement of ITs developed by rpg mutants, indicative of a loss of unidirectional polarized growth, is well explained by the failure of rpg-1 to maintain the typical VPY punctate localization observed in WT root hairs.
source: Moreover, the peculiar enlargement of ITs developed by rpg mutants, indicative of a loss of unidirectional polarized growth, is well explained by the failure of rpg-1 to maintain the typical VPY punctate localization observed in WT root hairs (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the IT phenotype and VPY localization data.

claim: Infectosome-like and VPY-positive compartments have also been observed during the AM symbiosis.
source: Interestingly, infectosome-like and VPY-positive compartments have also been observed during the AM symbiosis (Pumplin et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim cites Pumplin et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: vpy mutants exhibit strong defects in the AM symbiosis.
source: and vpy mutants exhibit strong defects in this association (Feddermann et al., 2010; Pumplin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim cites Feddermann et al., 2010 and Pumplin et al., 2010.

claim: The accumulation of VPY in infectosome-like compartments seems more important for full arbuscule development rather than for controlling initial fungal infections.
source: Functionally, the accumulation of VPY in such compartments seems more important for full arbuscule development rather than for controlling initial fungal infections (Lindsay et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Lindsay et al., 2022.

claim: The correlation between loss of VPY-recruitment into infectosome foci in the rpg mutant and its strong infection defects argues for a higher relevance, and perhaps extended function, of these cytoplasmic structures during bacterial accommodation.
source: In contrast, the correlation between loss of VPY-recruitment into infectosome foci in the rpg mutant and its strong infection defects (Figure 1B–C and Figure 4A–B) argues for a higher relevance, and perhaps extended function, of these cytoplasmic structures during bacterial accommodation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the VPY localization and IT phenotype data.

claim: RPG serves as a specificity determinant for infectosome-related endo- and exocytotic events during RNS.
source: In line with this, we hypothesize that RPG serves as a specificity determinant for infectosome-related endo- and exocytotic events during RNS (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is a proposed hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: RPG is transcriptionally dependent on NIN.
source: This is further supported by the transcriptional dependency of RPG from NIN (Liu et al., 2019a; Soyano and Hayashi, 2014)
evidence: The claim cites Liu et al., 2019a and Soyano and Hayashi, 2014.

claim: RPG is one of the few essential factors that have been lost in non-nodulating species of the FaFaCuRo clade.
source: and is in line with RPG being one of the few essential factors that have been lost in non-nodulating species of the FaFaCuRo clade (Griesmann et al., 2018; van Velzen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Griesmann et al., 2018 and van Velzen et al., 2018.

claim: Upon recruitment of VPY into the infectosome complex, it is further stabilized by LIN.
source: Upon recruitment of VPY into the infectosome complex, it is further stabilized by LIN (Liu et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim cites Liu et al., 2019b.

claim: CERBERUS, the ortholog of LIN in L. japonicus, has been shown to stabilize VPY protein levels.
source: This can also be assumed for CERBERUS, the ortholog of LIN in L. japonicus, which has been shown to stabilize VPY protein levels (Liu et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim cites Liu et al., 2021.

claim: CERBERUS interacts with RPG in L. japonicus.
source: and to interact with RPG in this closely related legume (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim cites Li et al., 2023.

claim: The genes encoding for VPY and LIN are retained in angiosperm species forming intracellular symbioses, together with those encoding for the central components of the common symbiosis signaling pathway CCaMK and CYCLOPS, which are essential for both AM and RNS.
source: Different from RPG, the genes encoding for VPY and LIN are retained in angiosperm species forming intracellular symbioses, together with those encoding for the central components of the common symbiosis signaling pathway CCaMK and CYCLOPS, which are essential for both AM and RNS (Radhakrishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Radhakrishnan et al., 2020.

claim: VPY was recently proposed to coordinate signaling and cellular accommodation during AM by negatively regulating the nuclear-localized symbiosis signaling kinase CCaMK via direct interaction.
source: Intriguingly, VPY was recently proposed to coordinate signaling and cellular accommodation during AM by negatively regulating the nuclear-localized symbiosis signaling kinase CCaMK via direct interaction (Lindsay et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Lindsay et al., 2022.

claim: If the regulatory function of VPY on CCaMK would be conserved during rhizobial infection, the ability of RPG to sequester VPY to cytoplasmic foci might additionally represent a way to modulate the input/output of a conserved endosymbiotic signaling circuit to adequately mediate bacterial infection.
source: If such regulatory function would be conserved during rhizobial infection, the ability of RPG to sequester VPY to cytoplasmic foci might additionally represent a way to modulate the input/output of a conserved endosymbiotic signaling circuit to adequately mediate bacterial infection (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the VPY-CCaMK interaction in AM.

claim: It is tempting to draw parallels between infectosomes and the 'polarisome,' a macromolecular complex coordinating the polarized growth of yeasts and fungal hyphae.
source: It is, however, tempting to draw parallels to the so-called 'polarisome,' a macromolecular complex coordinating the polarized growth of yeasts and fungal hyphae (Xie and Miao, 2021).
evidence: The claim is speculative and cites Xie and Miao, 2021.

claim: Polarisomes are dense spot-like structures localized at the site of polarized growth and are formed by a number of core components and many cooperative interactors.
source: Polarisomes are dense spot-like structures localized at the site of polarized growth and are formed by a number of core components and many cooperative interactors (Xie and Miao, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Xie and Miao, 2021.

claim: The polarisome is required to maintain the Spitzenkörper, a vesicle supply center located at the tip during hyphal growth, whose positioning is correlated with growth directionality.
source: The polarisome is also required to maintain the Spitzenkörper (Crampin et al., 2005), a vesicle supply center located at the tip during hyphal growth, whose positioning is correlated with growth directionality (Riquelme and Sánchez-León, 2014).
evidence: The claim cites Crampin et al., 2005 and Riquelme and Sánchez-León, 2014.

claim: A myosin protein has recently been shown to mediate focal packing of the polarisome.
source: Interestingly, a myosin protein has recently been shown to mediate focal packing of the polarisome (Dünkler et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Dünkler et al., 2021.

claim: The structural similarity of the RPG C-terminal extension with myosins, and the RPG-dependent recruitment of VPY into discrete cytoplasmic foci, further supports the hypothesis that RPG functions as an organizational hub protein for infectosome assembly and polarity maintenance during intracellular rhizobial infections.
source: The structural similarity of the RPG C-terminal extension with myosins, as supported by structural predictions and as previously suggested (Arrighi et al., 2008), and the RPG-dependent recruitment of VPY into discrete cytoplasmic foci (Figure 4A–F), further supports the hypothesis that RPG functions as an organizational hub protein for infectosome assembly and polarity maintenance during intracellular rhizobial infections (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is a proposed hypothesis based on structural similarity and the findings, and cites Arrighi et al., 2008.

claim: Rendering the infectosome complex dysfunctional in rpg mutants results in the loss of the highly polarized membrane enrichment of PI(4,5)P2 at the IT tip and unconfined secretion of key factors such as NPL required for IT progression to the growing IT tip.
source: Rendering the infectosome complex dysfunctional in rpg mutants results in the loss of the highly polarized membrane enrichment of PI(4,5)P2 at the IT tip (Figure 5A–C) and unconfined secretion of key factors such as NPL (Figure 6D–F) required for IT progression to the growing IT tip (Liu et al., 2019a; Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings and cites Liu et al., 2019a and Xie et al., 2012.

claim: In many eukaryotic polarized systems, localized exocytosis targets PI(4,5)P2-rich membrane domains.
source: As in many eukaryotic polarized systems, where localized exocytosis targets PI(4,5)P2-rich membrane domains,
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of eukaryotic cell biology.

claim: Accumulation of PI(4,5)P2 was shown to occur on perimicrobial membranes during pathogenic infections.
source: accumulation of this phosphoinositide was also shown to occur on perimicrobial membranes during pathogenic infections (Qin et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim cites Qin et al., 2020.

claim: During AM symbiosis, PI(4,5)P2 specifically accumulated at the tips of intracellular linear hyphae.
source: and during AM symbiosis, where PI(4,5)P2 specifically accumulated at the tips of intracellular linear hyphae (Ivanov and Harrison, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites Ivanov and Harrison, 2019.

claim: The generation of PI(4,5)P2 involves the phosphorylation of position 5 of PI4P catalyzed by phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate 5-kinases (PIP5K) localized at the plasma membrane and in the nucleus.
source: In eukaryotes, the generation of PI(4,5)P2 involves the phosphorylation of position 5 of PI4P catalyzed by phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate 5-kinases (PIP5K) localized at the plasma membrane and in the nucleus (Colin and Jaillais, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Colin and Jaillais, 2020.

claim: At least ten genes encoding for isoforms of PIP5K are contained in the Medicago genome and two of them are induced during infection thread development within root hairs.
source: At least ten genes encoding for isoforms of this enzyme are contained in the Medicago genome and, interestingly, two of them are induced during infection thread development within root hairs (Medtr3g073100, Medtr7g089950; Liu et al., 2019a), one of which (Medtr7g089950) in a NIN-dependent manner (Liu et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data and cites Liu et al., 2019a.

claim: Increased PI(4,5)P2 accumulation during infection might occur, at least in part, via transcriptional upregulation of its biosynthetic enzymes.
source: This further supports our data and suggests that increased PI(4,5)P2 accumulation during infection might occur, at least in part, via transcriptional upregulation of its biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the gene expression data.

claim: The trafficking/activity of PI(4,5)P2-metabolizing enzymes are also likely to contribute to the observed membrane enrichment, which is possibly a result of complex feedback loops occurring between those enzymes and their protein effectors such as small GTPases.
source: However, the trafficking/activity of these and/or other PI(4,5)P2-metabolizing enzymes are also likely to contribute to the observed membrane enrichment, which is possibly a result of complex feedback loops occurring between those enzymes and their protein effectors such as, for instance, small GTPases, as reported for other systems (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006).
evidence: The claim is speculative and cites Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006.

claim: A ROP (Rho of a plant) GTPase and its GEF effector were shown to be required for infection thread growth in L. japonicus.
source: In line with this, a ROP (Rho of a plant) GTPase and its GEF effector were shown to be required for infection thread growth in L. japonicus (Liu et al., 2020),
evidence: The claim cites Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Expression of at least one gene encoding for a RopGEF is induced during IC and IT formation in Medicago.
source: and expression of at least one gene encoding for a RopGEF is induced during IC and IT formation in Medicago (Breakspear et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim cites Breakspear et al., 2014.

claim: The generation of a stably polarized cell arises from the functional interplay between membrane-associated polarity circuits and consequent downstream cellular reorganization, with localized exocytosis being central to the process of tip growth.
source: Ultimately, the generation of a stably polarized cell arises from the functional interplay between membrane-associated polarity circuits and consequent downstream cellular reorganization (Ramalho et al., 2022), with localized exocytosis being central to the process of tip growth, as shown for pollen tube growth guidance in Arabidopsis (Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Ramalho et al., 2022 and Luo et al., 2017.

claim: Maintenance of the IC and secretion of NPL into the symbiotic apoplastic compartment is unaltered in rpg mutants, but remains unconfined.
source: It is noteworthy that maintenance of the IC and secretion of NPL into the symbiotic apoplastic compartment is unaltered in rpg mutants, but remains unconfined (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by NPL localization data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: The capacity of RPG to interact with EXO70H4 residing within infectosome foci is compatible with a model where RPG-mediated recruitment of this exocyst subunit could contribute to restrict the tethering of exocytotic vesicles at a single focal site to enable rapid tip growth and IT extension.
source: The capacity of RPG to interact with EXO70H4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 7) residing within infectosome foci (Liu et al., 2019b) is compatible with a model where RPG-mediated recruitment of this exocyst subunit could contribute to restrict the tethering of exocytotic vesicles at a single focal site to enable rapid tip growth and IT extension.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the interaction data and cites Liu et al., 2019b.

claim: In the absence of functional RPG, the slow growth caused by unrestricted secretion might negatively feedback on membrane polarization, as shown in yeast and fungi, where reduced growth rates have been linked to the destabilization of polar domains.
source: In the absence of functional RPG, the slow growth caused by unrestricted secretion might negatively feedback on membrane polarization, as shown in yeast and fungi, where reduced growth rates have been linked to the destabilization of polar domains (Haupt et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative and cites Haupt et al., 2018.

claim: Depolarization might alter the cytoskeleton organization with consequent loss of active polar tip growth.
source: Such depolarization might, in turn, alter the cytoskeleton organization with consequent loss of active polar tip growth.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings.

claim: Alongside with an alteration of the microtubule-based connectivity between the IT and the nucleus, it is likely that actin rearrangements might as well be affected.
source: Alongside with an alteration of the microtubule-based connectivity between the IT and the nucleus (Figure 6A–C), it is likely that actin rearrangements might as well be affected.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the microtubule data.

claim: Several genes encoding for actin remodeling proteins were reported to be important for IT growth.
source: While the organization of the actin cytoskeleton during infection thread progression will have to be investigated, several genes encoding for actin remodeling proteins were reported to be important for IT growth (Liang et al., 2021; Hossain et al., 2012; Yokota et al., 2009; Qiu et al., 2015; Miyahara et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim cites Liang et al., 2021, Hossain et al., 2012, Yokota et al., 2009, Qiu et al., 2015, and Miyahara et al., 2010.

claim: Actin dynamics were recently shown to be reduced upon inducible depletion of PI(4,5)P2 in Arabidopsis root cells.
source: and actin dynamics were recently shown to be reduced upon inducible depletion of PI(4,5)P2 in Arabidopsis root cells (Doumane et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Doumane et al., 2021.

claim: IT polarity requires few specific factors like RPG but predominantly relies on a highly conserved mechanism.
source: Taken together, our data strongly support the hypothesis that IT polarity requires few specific factors like RPG but predominantly relies on a highly conserved mechanism as suggested earlier (Gage, 2004; Yamazaki and Hayashi, 2015).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings and cites Gage, 2004 and Yamazaki and Hayashi, 2015.

claim: While the secretion domain in curled root hairs comprises the entire IC, the loss of highly restricted focal polarization results in uncoordinated expansion of such compartment and failure to maintain IT elongation.
source: While the secretion domain in curled root hairs comprises the entire IC (Fournier et al., 2015), the loss of highly restricted focal polarization results in uncoordinated expansion of such compartment and failure to maintain IT elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings and cites Fournier et al., 2015.

claim: While thin and elongated ITs are formed in root hairs of WT over the time period of live-cell imaging analysis (4–8 dpi), the growth of infection structures developed within root hairs of the rpg-1 mutant appears retarded and their shape is highly variable and irregular.
source: Indeed, while thin and elongated ITs are formed in root hairs of WT over the time period of our live-cell imaging analysis (4–8 dpi), the growth of infection structures developed within root hairs of the rpg-1 mutant appears retarded and their shape is highly variable and irregular (Figure 4A, Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data.

claim: Continuous multiplication of bacteria within rpg-1 infection structures likely leads to their slow and unguided progression across root hairs.
source: Continuous multiplication of bacteria within these structures then likely leads to their slow and unguided progression across root hairs (Figure 1B–D), as previously suggested (Arrighi et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings and cites Arrighi et al., 2008.

claim: The progressive disintegration of the EMT array and the increase distancing between the nucleus and the IT tip are indicative of aborted active growth.
source: and further supported by the progressive disintegration of the EMT array and the increase distancing between the nucleus and the IT tip (Figure 6A–C), indicative of aborted active growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the microtubule and tip-to-nucleus distance data.

claim: Although polarization of the basal membrane domain in the respective trichoblasts and formation of PITs in the outer cortical cells are unaltered in rpg-1, effective infection of nodules is impaired.
source: Although polarization of the basal membrane domain in the respective trichoblasts and formation of PITs in the outer cortical cells are unaltered (Figure 4A, Arrighi et al., 2008), effective infection of nodules is impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B),
evidence: The claim is supported by the findings and cites Arrighi et al., 2008.

claim: A strictly defined time window that allows transcellular IT growth through recently divided cells is likely missed by slowly growing ITs in the rpg mutant.
source: likely because a strictly defined time window that allows transcellular IT growth through recently divided cells is missed by these slowly growing ITs in the rpg mutant.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings.

claim: The temporal confinement of cellular infectability coupled with the highly controlled and paced growth of ITs represents an essential layer of host control over intracellularly progressing microbes.
source: While the molecular nature of this time window remains unknown, this temporal confinement of cellular infectability coupled with the highly controlled and paced growth of ITs represents an essential layer of host control over intracellularly progressing microbes.
evidence: The claim is a proposed interpretation of the findings.
